https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.title: The Times view on Just Stop Oil: In the Soup
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/the-tim.text:
Among Just Stop Oil’s more galling habits is their tendency to think of their cause as an exception to the norms of democratic life that bind everyone else. Convinced of their own righteousness, the movement’s footsoldiers think they have a licence to disrupt the lives of their fellow citizens and inflict indiscriminate damage on cultural artefacts.
Fortunately, the justice system takes a different view: a belief in one’s own moral superiority, ­however fervently held, affords no exemption under the law. In July, Just Stop Oil’s founder, ­Roger Hallam, and four of his fellow antagonists were handed custodial sentences of record length after disrupting traffic on the M25. This week, equally deserved prison sentences were handed to two activists who threw Heinz tomato soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers in 2022. In sentencing the pair, the judge recognised not only the thousands of pounds worth of damage done to the painting’s 17th-century frame, on which the soup acted as a “paint stripper”, but also the harm that might have been done had soup seeped behind the glass.
Despite Just Stop Oil’s general insistence on mankind taking full responsibility for the ­consequences of its actions, the movement is ­oddly unwilling to apply the maxim to itself. This week, a letter signed by celebrities including the actress Juliet Stevenson argued that the pair should be spared jail on the contorted grounds that their vandalism constituted a “Pollock-esque” contribution to the“well-established tradition of creative iconoclasm”. An artful excuse, indeed.
These public figures should be shamed by the antisocial criminality they seek to excuse. ­On Friday, in an apparent copy-cat attack, three Just Stop Oil activists again threw soup over two Van Goghs in the National Gallery. The protesters involved should reflect that when artists begin to repeat themselves, it may be time to retire.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Green backers helped Labour amass £26m in run-up to election
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Businesses including Quadrature Capital and Ecotricity — a former backer of Just Stop Oil — donated millions to Sir Keir Starmer’s campaign
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Labour raised £26 million in the run-up to the general election, more than 50 per cent more than the Tories, thanks in part to big donations from green backers.
The party received £4 million from Quadrature Capital, a hedge fund, which said the donation was intended to “support policies that will deliver climate action”. Quadrature Capital has pledged to give $325 million a year to combat climate change. The company’s 113 staff are paid an average of £3 million each.
Labour also received £2 million from Ecotricity, the company founded by the campaigner Dale Vince. In the past has Vince funded the campaign group Just Stop Oil, but he withdrew his support last year.
Another £2.5 million came from Lord Sainsbury of Turville, a longstanding Labour donor. The bulk of Labour’s income came from individuals and companies, and £5.6 million was from trade unions. The Tories received just over £16 million in the second quarter of 2024, including £5 million from Frank Hester, the donor embroiled in a racism row. In total Hester gave the Tories £10 million in the run-up to the general election.
The Tories also received £1.25 million from Access Industries, a company owned by the oil tycoon Sir Leonard Blavatnik. The Liberal Democrats raised nearly £6 million and Reform UK, which won five seats at the election, raised £2.6 million.
The Tories had hoped to gain an advantage by calling an early election, but in the event Labour succeeded in bringing in more donations and winning the social media battle.
Labour said that the run-up to the election had been its “best-performing quarter ever” for individual donations. Ellie Reeves, chairwoman of the Labour Party, said: “Thanks to Keir Starmer’s leadership, the Labour Party experienced the largest financial boost from individual donations ever in the lead-up to the general election.
“The scale and breadth of support received reflects the widespread support for a Labour Party which campaigned on five missions to transform Britain and has a serious plan to deliver for working people. Keir Starmer has put the British people at the heart of our government and has already begun the important work of fixing the foundations of the country.”
Quadrature Capital said: “In May 2024, we came to the view that a UK government with a commitment to the green transition of the economy would have the ability to drive change that is so urgently needed. Having analysed commitments set out by each party, we donated £4 million to the Labour Party, in support of policies that will deliver climate action while also promoting social equity and economic resilience. This was a values-based donation, not a political donation.”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Art vandals echo the witchfinder general
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
No sooner were the Van Gogh vandals jailed than others, albeit with a different flavour of soup, did it again. This time two of those arrested were older adults but although the retired are well represented, climate activism has notably recruited youth ever since Greta Thunberg’s first school strike. Gaza and gender protests show a similar pattern of indignation: those aged 16 to 24 are barely 11 per cent of the population but estimated as roughly a third of demonstrators.
Older generations recall 1960s Vietnam, civil rights and university demos fuelled by young blood. All ages hit the streets at times but youth is better at scaling buildings and tolerating crowds, less preoccupied with daily responsibilities and fears and easily frustrated by any world built by its elders.
Fair enough: we’re all frustrated, but eventually we mesh into the system by canvassing and voting or channel it into charity or community efforts. But in the impatient youngest there can easily rise something darker and deeper: the leading edge of real fanaticism. Some Extinction Rebellion videos show it in their cavalier dismissal of others’ rights; some Palestine campaigners tip over into violent intent, as do gender-identity extremists, Islamist jihadis and teenagers who threaten asylum hotels.
• Richard Morrison: How to deter the art vandals — punish them properly
Every time you see such hot, bold spirits hurling themselves into the blessed relief of righteousness, you notice the older adult figures behind them. A few are there to identify out of vanity (look at those XR celebrity backers flying in to show how they hate fossil fuel). But many are actively exploiting that ever-renewing spring of beautiful vigour: they’re running an emotional Ponzi scheme that sucks in the cheap energy of youth with dubious promises.
I was reflecting on this because of a remarkable new play by Joanna Carrick which reaches the capital — Southwark Playhouse — in a few weeks’ time. I saw The Ungodly, a small dramatic powerhouse, a year ago in Ipswich. Its roots are in local history, tightly researched in parish records but explored and “workshopped” during Covid in community work and audio productions, including disabled people and inmates at HMP Warren Hill.
It deals with the dark period in the early 1640s when, within three years, more women were hanged as witches than in the previous 160, the whole religious Reformation. The key figure is Matthew Hopkins, the self-appointed witchfinder general.
What I had never realised is that this figure’s reign of terror began when he was 24 and ended with his death three years later. His fanaticism was fed by Puritan “lecturers”, and the fragility of his audience aggravated by crop and cattle failures and high infant mortality. In a remote agricultural community, ruin always looms and scapegoating is tempting. An old lady muttering crossly to herself might be uttering a curse; let her name her cat oddly and you suspect it of being Satan’s spirit manifesting through “condensed and thickened air”.
• The Times view on Just Stop Oil: In the Soup
But central to this particular cataclysm of suspicion and persecution was the fire burning in Hopkins: portrayed growing up as a geeky, insecure, stammering teenager who hated his tavern job, repelled by coarse older drunkards and uneasy with the frank sexual carnality of farmhouse life.
He is not like the hysterical girls in The Crucible: his puritanism is more like calm relief, an achieved identity that simplifies the universe. Point the finger, condemn the target as evil and quote “You shall not suffer a witch to live” from the Book of Exodus — though actually that’s only one line, oddly sandwiched between rules on debt and dowries and a ban on bestiality. With extreme Puritans the Bible is always the Old Testament; none of that soft Jesus reluctance to cast the first stone. When the poor old women get rounded up, the young witchfinder’s worried half-sister Susan asks him: “Will they hang? All?” He replies: “They must!”
It’s a fascinating play, with echoes impossible to ignore. Not only because of the dangerous certainties everywhere today but because headlong youthful conviction is a perennial phenomenon requiring respect and containment. It holds both hopeful beauty and malicious danger, and anyone with spirit remembers it burning, even for a football team or pop idol.
At my convent school (in Tunbridge Wells), despite the Cold War artful nuns invited a communist speaker to the sixth form, perhaps as a homeopathic dose. He wore purple gym shoes and gave us all pocket-sized Communist Manifestos. I well remember the excitement of Marx’s prose.
The passion of recruited youth has fed honourable causes. Think of the International Brigades in 1930s Spain, of the Arab Spring, Jan Palach in Wenceslas Square. It serves armies too, for good or ill: here’s Rupert Brooke in 1914 thanking God that wartime “caught our youth, and wakened us from sleeping … as swimmers into cleanness leaping, glad from a world grown old and cold and weary”.
We, the old and cold and weary, may be exasperated by soup-flingers, scared by jihadis and scornful of the hysteria against JK Rowling. But it is not enough to condemn or mock kids whose rage against fossil fuel is accompanied by selfies from exotic holidays.
From the multi-cause ranting of Thunberg to the proselytising Islamism that made Salman Abedi the Manchester bomber at 22, sapling passion requires attention. Demonisation doesn’t help, nor does the affectionate defence of criminality from many arrested children’s parents (“She’s a passionate spirit”). Only interest, calm evidence, steady respectful argument.
My convent-commie phase, by the way, was eventually dampened by reading about Stalin.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Just Stop Oil activists who threw soup over Van Gogh masterpiece jailed
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland damaged the antique frame of Sunflowers during their protest against climate change at the National Gallery in 2022
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Two Just Stop Oil activists have been jailed for throwing tomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and damaging its antique frame.
Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland, both 22, threw two tins of Heinz tomato soup at the painting at the National Gallery and then glued themselves to the wall in October 2022 in the group’s high-profile stunt. Plummer was jailed for two years and Holland for 20 months.
While the painting, which was completed in 1888 and is worth up to £72.5 million, was protected by a glass cover, prosecutors believe the soup, which is said to have acted as a “paint stripper”, may have caused £10,000 worth of damage to its 17th-century Italian frame.
• Van Gogh at the National Gallery: masterpieces no one has ever matched
The activists, who denied damaging property, showed no emotion as the jury announced its verdict after a four-day trial at Southwark crown court in July. Judge Christopher Hehir released them on bail before sentencing on Friday. Hehir told them to come to court “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison on that date”.
The maximum sentence for the offence is ten years’ imprisonment. The bail conditions stipulate that they must not carry glue, paint or any adhesive substance in a public place and must not visit any galleries or museums.
The court was told that the pair had visited the museum a day before the incident to carry out reconnaissance and had bought the soup from a supermarket.
In a statement read to the jury, Isabella Kocum, a frame conservator, said she was “shocked and dismayed by the extent of corrosion this tomato soup” caused to the “exquisite antique frame”.
She told the court: “The frame was specifically chosen for Van Gogh’s painting because of the matching colouration. I remain amazed at how corrosive the soup was to the frame. Even once the majority of the soup had been removed, I was alarmed to see that the remainder was acting like a paint stripper in front of my eyes.”
• Climate and war protests eat into real policing, says Met boss
Plummer, who studied at the University of Manchester and represented herself at the trial, told the court that she decided to use tomato soup “because it would stand out” and that it “symbolised the link between the climate crisis and the cost of living crisis”.
The activists denied that they considered the frame when planning and carrying out the protest and told the court that they believed the painting would be protected by the glass cover.
Plummer and Holland said they were taking instructions from someone else in Just Stop Oil but refused to identify the person.
Plummer told the jury that she loved the painting. In her closing speech, she claimed that she was “sounding an alarm bell” on climate change and invoked the example of the suffragettes and the civil rights movement in the United States.
She said: “I don’t think that action like this fits the black and white letter of the law. Sometimes morality is different from the law, different from justice, different from legal directions. We caused some damage to the frame. The painting was returned to the gallery the same day.
“The frame has not been further restored since then. The frame was not damaged enough to warrant further restoration. It is still deemed worthy to encase a precious, priceless work of art. I intended to shine a light on the climate crisis and on the cost of living crisis.”
On Thursday, more than a hundred artists, curators and historians called for the activists to be spared jail because they had upheld a “centuries-old tradition of calling on our social conscience through art”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Don’t jail activists over ‘creative’ Van Gogh soup protest, artists urge
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: More than 100 artists, curators and art historians have signed a letter saying the Just Stop Oil protest was in the tradition of Banksy and the suffragettes
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Two environmental activists who threw tomato soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers should be spared jail because their actions belong to the “well-established tradition of creative iconoclasm”, a group of art professionals have said.
In October 2022, Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland, both 22, were filmed throwing two tins of Heinz tomato soup over the 19th-century masterpiece at the National Gallery in central London.
Earlier this year they were found guilty of criminal damage after the court was told that the soup caused an estimated £10,000 worth of damage to the picture’s frame.
They will be sentenced on Friday with Judge Christopher Hehir previously telling them to come “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison”.
Before their court date a group of more than 100 artists, curators and art historians have signed a letter likening the Just Stop Oil activists to the suffragettes, and said their actions will “enrich the story and social meaning of Sunflowers”.
• ‘We’re not criminals’: what Just Stop Oil’s poster girls told me
Signatories include Juliet Stevenson, the actress, Jonathan Barnbrook, who helped design David Bowie’s album covers, and academics from Copenhagen University, Goldsmiths and Queen Mary University of London.
In the letter, which was co-ordinated by Greenpeace UK, they said the act “connects entirely to the artistic canon” of iconoclasm — the rejection or destruction of images or monuments often for religious or political reasons.
It then went on to compare the actions with the graffiti of Banksy, the German artist Gustav Metzger and his auto-destructive art and the modification paintings of Asger Jorn.
“The work of all these iconoclasts, often far more physically destructive than the work of JSO [Just Stop Oil], is now venerated in museums around the world,” the letter said.
They also praised the soup-covered artwork saying it made the painting resemble an abstract Jackson Pollock-style piece.
“Plummer and Holland knew the painting was protected from the soup by a solid pane of glass when they threw the red-orange missive making a Pollock-esque splatter across the mustard yellow, drooping blooms.
“Their iconoclasm was temporary, a sight to behold to make their protest,” they added. “Judge Hehir should refrain from punishing Plummer and Holland with custodial sentences for upholding a centuries’ old tradition of calling on our social conscience through art.”
Hehir, who will deliver the sentence on Friday at Southwark Crown Court, previously told the pair they “came within the width of a pane of glass of destroying one of the most valuable artworks in the world”.
He is the same judge who recently gave five environmental activists who forced the M25 to close jail terms of more than four years — believed to be a record for non-violent protest.
The lengthy sentences prompted concern from a number of prominent politicians, celebrities and environmentalists.
Both Plummer and Holland are long-standing members of Just Stop Oil, which is demanding an end to all new oil and gas licences, and have been arrested a number of times.
Plummer, a former Manchester University student, was arrested at Heathrow Airport last month — days after being found guilty for the Van Gogh incident — after spraying departure boards and windows orange.
Speaking to The Times in July, she said she felt “empowered” after throwing the soup at Sunflowers.
“I felt like I was seizing back power from the systems that are hell-bent on destroying us and destroying everything we know and love,” she said.
Holland added: “The fact of the matter is, as a result of our action, people are talking about not just what we did, but about the demands that we are conveying as Just Stop Oil.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Cumbria coalmine plan blocked by High Court
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Decision to approve Whitehaven site in 2022 deemed ‘legally flawed’ after Supreme Court’s ruling on future carbon emissions
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
The construction of Britain’s first new coal mine in 30 years has been blocked by the High Court in what campaigners have hailed as a “huge victory for the environment”.
The decision is the first since a Supreme Court ruling stating that future fossil fuel emissions must be considered in planning applications for new extraction projects.
The Whitehaven mine in Cumbria was approved by Michael Gove in 2022 to supply coal for steel manufacturing. However in a ruling published on Friday, Justice Holgate said giving the go-ahead for the development was “legally flawed”.
The new government had informed the court that planning permission should be quashed, but the case proceeded because the mine’s developer, West Cumbria Mining (WCM), wanted to defend the original decision. The company argued that it planned to build a “unique net zero” mine that would provide coking coal for high-quality steel needed to build wind turbines, electric vehicles or trains.
Friends of the Earth and South Lakes Action on Climate Change (SLACC) had challenged the Whitehaven plan, arguing that it did not take into account carbon dioxide emissions over the plant’s lifetime.
The case against the mine was given a significant boost by the Supreme Court’s landmark Finch ruling in June, which found that Surrey county council should have taken overall emissions into account when approving plans for an oil drilling project in Horse Hill.
That ruling, which legal experts warned would leave other carbon intensive projects vulnerable to legal challenges, prompted Angela Rayner to abandon the government’s defence of the Whitehaven proposal on the basis that it should not have received planning permission in the first place.
Coal extracted from the proposed mine had been earmarked for use in steelmaking, although critics warned that much of it would likely end up being exported. The UK’s biggest steelworks at Port Talbot is in the process of transitioning away from coal-powered blast furnaces towards electric arc furnaces as part of a £500 million deal agreed this week with the government.
Paul Brown KC, for Friends of the Earth, said in written submissions that there was “no significant need for the coal” in the UK. He added that the decision to approve the mine “smacked of hypocrisy” given the UK’s “vocal international advocacy” over the phase-out of coal.
James Strachan, for the mine’s developer, said the arguments in the legal challenge were “poorly disguised attacks on the planning judgments made by the inspector and the secretary of state”.
However, in a 48-page ruling, the judge said those approving the development “failed to deal” with the fact that “a positive precedent effect of a net-zero mine leading to other similar projects would depend upon further offsetting arrangements”, adding “that would be undesirable because offsets are a finite resource”.
WMC said it “will consider the implications of the High Court judgment”.
Niall Toru, a senior lawyer at Friends of the Earth, described it as “fantastic news and a huge victory for our environment and everyone who has fought against this climate-damaging and completely unnecessary coalmine”.
He added: “That the ruling today has gone against the mining company could have ramifications internationally, as there are cases abroad where challenges are being made against fossil fuel projects on a very similar basis.”
Dr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist, said: “Coal mining belongs in the past, so hopefully this is the last we’ll hear of it. The UK government now needs to ensure communities right across [the] country aren’t left with [the] choice of high-carbon jobs or no jobs.”
The ruling comes in the wake of news that 2,500 people are set to be made redundant at the Port Talbot steelworks as it transitions to greener electric technology.
Jonathan Reynolds has agreed for the government to provide £500 million funding towards the construction of a new greener electric arc furnace at the site, with the plant’s Indian owners, Tata Steel, putting in £750 million.
Those made redundant will receive better terms under an “improved” deal, which amends an agreement made by the previous Conservative administration.
The Conservatives said Labour had raised “false hopes” about saving jobs. Trade unions said the plan was “not something to celebrate” but was “better than the devastating plan announced by Tata and the Tories back in September 2023”.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-l.title: Times letters: Murder case failings and pressure on police
https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-l.text:
Sir, This haunting case brings together the institutional failures of the Metropolitan Police that have been obvious for years (“Police in dock over murder of two women by predator”, Sep 19). Once again the organisation appears to have failed in three crucially important areas.
First, it has not sufficiently changed its approach to the black community. Second, it has not responded to domestic abuse as a priority and in a way known to work. Third, and fundamentally, it recruits senior leaders almost exclusively from its own pool of officers who breathe the culture every day and struggle to see beyond the “rules” of the “way we do business here”.
• Met failed to stop abuser killing one girlfriend — then they let it happen again
I know because I was one of those officers. It took me decades to start to see different possibilities. My education came from the Lawrence inquiry and women who understood domestic abuse. True leaders should know better and act differently and look beyond the hubristic belief in their own wisdom.Anthony WillsSuperintendent, Metropolitan Police 1997-2003; Thame, Oxon
Sir, Further to Fiona Hamilton’s analysis “Force’s failures haunt bereaved families” (Behind the story, Sep 19), until structural changes are made it is very difficult to see how “a new Met for London” is possible. Going back to basics is a part of this, including focusing on policing London and not on continuing as the police force for England and Wales.
One of the biggest obstacles to a better Metropolitan Police is the “Met knows best” syndrome. If other forces are improving their retention of experienced officers, hitting recruitment targets and resolving crimes faster despite facing the same funding pressures, why are the Met and Sadiq Khan not learning from these forces? New thinking for policing London is urgently needed.Festus AkinbusoyeBedfordshire police and crime commissioner 2021-24; London WC1
Sir, The pressures on the police are immense. In England and Wales there are more than 3,000 offences of violence against women and girls each day. In London, some detectives are handling 30 rape investigations each. The policing of Just Stop Oil, Notting Hill carnival and pro-Palestinian marches alone has taken 70,000 police officer shifts, amounting to half a million hours. In London, the Metropolitan Police faces an annual shortfall of £450 million; in England and Wales the figure is as high as £3.5 billion. Moreover, high-harm offences such as organised crime and sexual offences are increasingly complex to investigate
The New York police department receives 50 per cent more funding per officer than London, and New York is not a capital city. The public, through their elected policymakers, must decide how much threat, harm and risk they are prepared to tolerate. The police cannot do everything with the resources they have. If the public want to feel — and be — safer, they need to be prepared to pay for that.Sir Thomas WinsorChief inspector of constabulary 2012-22; East Grinstead, W Sussex
Sir, Sir Mark Rowley warns politicians that being openly critical of his force encourages the criminal fraternity and then goes on to describe how his force is “dangerously stretched” (“Politicians who accuse police ‘embolden thugs’ ”, Sep 19). If anything, knowing that the Met is in dire straits is more likely than politicians’ criticisms to give comfort to criminals. Rowley seems not to appreciate that, and ends up doing the very thing he was trying to prevent.Philip DimondBearsted, Kent
Sir, It seems some special advisers (Spads) have been forced to accept a pay cut on entering Whitehall. They are so angry that someone has leaked the revelation that the country’s top special adviser, Sue Gray, is being paid more than the prime minister (news, Sep 19). The new government should have learnt from what occurred when the coalition came to power in 2010. As a new special adviser in the Department for Business, I took on far more responsibility than I had ever faced before, while similarly being forced to take a cut in salary.
Back then, the civil service machine quickly came to regret squashing the confidence of new special advisers. After just a few days, our senior departmental officials were heard complaining that the new Spads were not throwing their weight around Whitehall in the same way as our better-paid predecessors had done.Nick HillmanHaddenham, Bucks
Sir, While I hold no particular brief for Sue Gray and am concerned about the influence of unelected special advisers, I find the fact that she is paid marginally more than the prime minister to be unsurprising. The near parity arises from the fact that the prime minister is grossly underpaid rather than the other way round.Richard MangnallPoundbury, Dorset
Sir, Of course Sue Gray needs a higher salary than the prime minister, as she has to pay for her own clothes, spectacles, tickets for football matches and entertainment gigs as well as money for clothes for her family members. In addition she doesn’t have government-provided accommodation or an entertainment allowance. I’m only surprised she didn’t ask for more.Mike EvansGuildford
Sir, Liz Brownsell’s article “Charity watchdog should support trustees — not just disqualify them” (comment, Sep 19) raises a critical point. The emphasis on disqualification is deterring individuals from becoming trustees, because the risks of personal liability and reputational damage loom large. Although maintaining public trust in charities is vital, the focus should be on offering more robust support and guidance to trustees, many of whom are volunteers.
The sector badly needs more trustees to step forward to service in what can be an immensely demanding but stressful role. But more should be done to encourage people to take on these roles without fear of harsh penalties for honest mistakes. A balance between accountability and proactive support would result in more confident, capable trustees, ultimately benefiting the charity sector.Phoebe WhitlockLay trustee, Royal Microscopical Society, and chair, board of trustees, Codebar
Sir, Recent comment articles about train drivers’ conditions of service have overlooked the increased productivity introduced since privatisation, which was the quid pro quo for the rates of pay now in place (“Modern railway must be price for higher pay”, Sep 11). Drivers now work longer shifts with greater flexibility.
If the industry had remained nationalised this would have meant all drivers being on the same pay and conditions. As it is, British Rail was fragmented into separate private companies each with different salaries and working practices. This made the attempts by the previous Conservative government to impose a “one size fits all” package of reforms completely impractical.
The pay offer from the Department for Transport accepted this week makes clear that “efficiency” and “productivity proposals” are on the table for the next round of pay talks, which will be conducted at company level. A far more sensible approach from the newly elected government.Edward MayneTrain driver, Birmingham
Sir, Katy Balls nails the Tories’ problem perfectly in saying that the likes of Robert Jenrick and Kemi Badendoch should not attempt to compete with Nigel Farage (“Tory beauty parade is really all about Farage”, Sep 19). Neither has the communication skills nor the warmth and clubbability that the Reform leader exudes. Moreover, attempting this to match Farage would kill any chance of the Tories returning to power within the next decade, as it would alienate mainstream voters.Charles TownleyHove, E Sussex
Sir, The article on scabies by Deborah Ross (“Scabies: a medical adventure”, Times2, Sep 19) reminded me of my first teaching position in Glasgow, in 1971. I picked up the disease from the children by using their pencils, which they had been sucking, to correct or amend their work. It was a humiliating experience. The school nurse had me strip off and “painted’ me from top to toe with some sort of deterrent, and I was immediately sent home, where I promptly managed to infect my mum and dad. It was not a pleasant experience.Geraldine BlakeWorthing, W Sussex
Sir, Falling childhood vaccination rates will come as no surprise to anyone who has recently attempted to get their child vaccinated (“How to give GPs a shot at raising child vaccination rates”, Thunderer, Sep 19). To book an appointment for my three-year-old to receive the second MMR jab, I spent 20 minutes waiting to speak to a receptionist, only to be told that a nurse would need to return my call the next day to arrange the slot — at an unspecified time, of course.
The appointments offered were more than three weeks away, all during working hours. The slot allocated was five minutes — not enough time for the nurse to explain what vaccines were being offered, let alone their potential benefits and side-effects. GPs and receptionists have been successful in gatekeeping access to services. Falling vaccination rates and the increased spread of childhood diseases such as measles are the result.Miriam Fine MillsLondon NW11
Sir, Stephen Fry’s view of retirement is both patronising and outdated (“I was called Celibate Stephen. I forgot to have sex”, Sep 18). Perhaps he should consider the many thousands of hours of unpaid child and social care that retired people contribute to the economy. And not to mention the umpteen classes and interests that they pursue, everything from art history to Zumba. Elasticated trousers? No need, we’re too fit. Countdown? Sorry, we’re far too busy.Patricia Knott (ret’d)Wimborne, Dorset
Sir, Aside from sadness at the loss of jobs for Tupperware employees (“Fate Sealed”, leading article, Sep 19), it is also a reflection of the way we eat and its effects on obesity. Nutritional, affordable food can be cooked at home, transported in Tupperware and eaten at work or school.You only have to look at Mumbai’s tiffin boxes to appreciate the value that Tupperware can provide.Charlotte GurneyDilham, Norfolk
Sir, Matthew Parris was lucky to be in the bottom bunk on his recent sleeper train to Inverness (notebook, Sep 18). Having recently travelled to Glasgow in similar accommodation (albeit in the top bunk), I found it well-nigh impossible to ascend the awkwardly placed and narrow-runged vertical ladder that incarcerated your correspondent without the aid of my shoes while performing contortions worthy of a much younger Olympian gymnast. Sloping, flat-stepped ladders on the Caledonian sleeper would have benefited us both immensely.John MitchellBishopton, Renfrewshire
Sir, I fear Giles Coren (“How these presenters say Kyiv is my pet peeve”, Sep 17; letter, Sep 18) will have a long wait for BBC presenters to pronounce Kyiv correctly. https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Environmentalists win chance to challenge North Sea oil and gas plan in court
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.subtitle: Greenpeace UK and Uplift say the impact of burning fossil fuels from Rosebank and Jackdaw must be taken into account
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
Two environmental organisations have been granted permission for a legal challenge on the Rosebank and Jackdaw offshore oil and gasfields.
Greenpeace UK and Uplift are arguing that the impact of emissions from burning the fossil fuels extracted was illegally ignored.
On November 12 they will state in court that Rosebank will damage a protected area in the North Sea and the surrounding marine life.
Both environmental organisations will bring separate legal challenges against the UK government’s decision to approve the oilfield, and will be heard in the Scottish Court of Session.
Mel Evans, the climate team leader of Greenpeace UK, said: “It’s welcome news that we have permission on all of our legal grounds to challenge Rosebank and Jackdaw in two months’ time.
“We will continue to fight the corporate greed of fossil fuel companies like Equinor, Shell and Ithaca, and we look forward to our day in court.
“Both the government and the Supreme Court agree that you cannot ignore the emissions generated from burning fossil fuels.
“Equinor, Shell and Ithaca know this, and they know that the consents for these fields are unlawful. But despite this they are continuing to develop them during this judicial review, putting people, marine life and our climate at further risk.”
She added: “Rosebank and Jackdaw will do nothing to help our energy security or bring down our bills — the oil and gas extracted will be sold on the international market, making these companies, their bosses and shareholders even richer.
“If it went ahead, the Rosebank oilfield could release as much carbon as 56 coal plants running for a year, costing UK taxpayers billions in subsidies while lining the pockets of its big-oil owners.
“And the Jackdaw field will produce more carbon dioxide than the annual emissions of Ghana.
“The oil companies are trying to hide this from the public and the government. That’s why we’re taking the fight to the oil companies in the Scottish courts in November.”
The Rosebank oilfield is to the west of Shetland and holds about 500 million barrels of oil equivalent, Uplift said.
The organisation says 90 per cent of its reserves are oil and the remainder is gas, and that burning all of it would amount to the release of 200 million tonnes of carbon dioxide.
Development of Rosebank has been delayed several times since its discovery in 2004, but in August 2022 the Norwegian oil company Equinor submitted an environmental statement to the UK government outlining its plans to develop the field, which triggered the start of the assessment process.
If the judicial reviews are successful, Uplift and Greenpeace will ask the court to quash the decisions to approve Rosebank, compelling the UK government to review its decision in line with the law.
The UK energy minister Michael Shanks said: “This government is committed to making Britain a clean-energy superpower, helping to meet our first mission to kick-start economic growth.
“While we make that transition, the oil and gas industry will play an important role in the economy for decades to come. As we support the North Sea’s clean energy future, this government is committed to protecting current and future generations of good jobs as we do so.”
Shanks said that Labour would “consult at pace” on new guidance that took into account the Supreme Court’s ruling on environmental impact assessments.
A spokesman for Equinor said: “Equinor, in principle, does not comment on ongoing litigation.“Equinor welcomed regulatory approvals for the Rosebank development in 2023 and will continue to work closely with all relevant parties to progress the project.“It is vital for the UK and will bring benefits in terms of local investment, jobs and energy security.”
Ithica and Uplift were approached for comment. Shell could not be reached for comment.
A spokesperson for Shell said: “The hearing was administrative and no decision was taken on the substance of the case. From the outset, Jackdaw has been developed in line with all relevant consents and permits. At the substantive hearing of the judicial review in November, Shell will argue that those existing consents to develop Jackdaw should remain in place.“We accept the Supreme Court’s ruling in the Finch case, but will argue that Jackdaw is a vital project for UK energy security that is already well under way. Stopping the work is a highly complex process, with significant technical and safety issues now that infrastructure is in place and drilling has started in the North Sea.“Jackdaw will provide fuel for UK customers — enough to heat 1.4 million homes — strengthening energy independence for Britain, as other older gas fields reach the end of production.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Campaigners call for review of ‘unlawful’ anti-protest legislation
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: A think tank has called on the Labour government to review the law that has been labelled ‘deeply troubling’ by the UN
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Protesters have felt the harsh slap of the law over recent months — in July five eco-warriors were handed prison sentences of up to five years for causing chaos on gantries above the M25 motorway.
Roger Hallam, the 58-year-old founder of the campaign group Just Stop Oil received the longest sentence, which is now being appealed amid claims that the terms breached international law and are longer than those handed to rioters.
The previous government attempted to crack down on protestors who aimed to cause maximum disruption to daily life by enacting legislation that significantly reduced the threshold at which the police could impose conditions on demonstrations.
• Just Stop Oil sentences will only strengthen resolve, jailed founder believes
Under legislation guided through parliament last year by the former home secretary, Suella Braverman KC, the police can now curb protests if they deem that the action will cause “serious disruption”. The legislation is aimed in part at stopping the blockading of roads and attacks on sporting events, tactics frequently invoked by groups such as Just Stop Oil, Extinction Rebellion and Insulate Britain.
Ministers at the time argued that there was also a financial cost to mass protests. A 13-week campaign by Just Stop Oil last summer was said to have cost the Metropolitan Police more than £7.7 million, the equivalent cost of 23,500 officer shifts.
Protestors convicted under the beefed-up law of intentionally or recklessly causing public nuisance can now be jailed for up to ten years. Sir Keir Starmer, as leader of the opposition, backed the law — but it was condemned by the UN human rights commissioner as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”. Dale Vince, a millionaire Labour donor, called on the party to intervene in the case.
And now campaigners are calling on the Labour government to review the still fresh legislation, which has been lambasted by a think tank as a “knee-jerk” response to public opinion.
Demos, a cross-party group, says in a report today that it had found “overwhelming support” among the public for the right to protest and that people’s views were “more nuanced” than simply being concerned about disruption.
The report, produced jointly with another civil liberties group, Liberty, calls for a “wide-ranging” independent review of protest legislation and the policing of protest. It comes after campaigners held workshops at which members of the public were given more time and information to reach “properly considered judgments”. As a result, the report’s authors say, concerns about disruption become “less prominent”.
“Too often, politicians have relied on knee-jerk public opinion, itself based on limited knowledge of the protest landscape,” says Polly Curtis, the chief executive of Demos.
She argues that by providing people with “balanced information and exposing them to different viewpoints, it’s clear that people’s views are far more nuanced and there is more consensus than recent clampdowns account for. The public recognises protest as a fundamental right and strongly believes it should be protected.”
Last month, Liberty accused the government of showing “disregard for the rule of law” after the Home Office instructed lawyers to appeal against a recent High Court ruling that anti-protest legislation had been created unlawfully.
The group argued that the legislation, which reduced the threshold for conditions to be imposed to “more than minor disruption”, was unlawful as it was enacted through a government statutory instrument after being rejected by parliament. Starmer’s government continued the appeal despite Richard Hermer KC, the attorney-general, stating that the government will not “abuse” secondary legislation.
And earlier this week, Andy Cooke, His Majesty’s Chief Inspector of Constabulary, said that Braverman had been wrong when as home secretary she criticised the Metropolitan Police publicly over its handling of pro-Palestine protests. An article she wrote in The Times accused the force of “double standards” and led to her sacking.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/greenpe.title: Greenpeace activists who scaled Rishi Sunak’s home walk free
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greenpe.subtitle: The judge has thrown out the case, saying the evidence against the four protesters was ‘so tenuous’ that no court would convict them
https://www.thetimes.com/article/greenpe.text:
Four environmental protesters who scaled Rishi Sunak’s home in Yorkshire and allegedly damaged the roof walked free after a judge threw out the charges citing “weak” and “tenuous” evidence.
Amy Rugg-Easey, 33, Alexandra Wilson, 32, Mathieu Soete, 38, and Michael Grant, 64, were accused of damaging 15 roof slates during the five-hour demonstration against new North Sea oil projects at the former prime minister’s grade II listed home in Kirby Sigston, North Yorkshire, last August.
During the protest, the activists, who were dressed in red overalls and safety helmets, climbed on to the roof using ladders and ropes shortly before 8am and draped 200m of black fabric over the house before displaying a large placard that read “No New Oil”.
Sunak, 44, his wife Akshata Murty, 44, and their two daughters were on holiday at the time.
The prosecution told the York magistrates’ court that the family were left with a bill of £2,937.86 to fix nine Westmorland and six Welsh Blue slates.
After the prosecution closed its case for causing criminal damage, Owen Greenhall, the activists’ lawyer, argued that there was no case to answer because it could not be proved the damage to the roof was caused during the protest.
In a decision handed down on Friday, Judge Adrian Lower said the evidence against the defendants was “so tenuous” that no court would convict them. He said he would deliver a full ruling on November 11.
The court was told that Malcolm Richardson, a foreman and experienced roofer with a contract to carry out work at Sunak’s home, was called to inspect the roof after a police officer investigating the protest said he believed there had been some damage.
Richardson said he was asked to inspect only the area where he was told the protesters had been and identified 15 tiles that would need to be repaired.
In a statement to police, he claimed he could tell the damage was recent because of “weathering and colouration”. Pictures taken by the roofer were used by the prosecution, who said it was evident “that the location of the damage corresponds to the locations where the defendants went”.
While Richardson was giving evidence, it was revealed that three of the 15 pictures used by the prosecution were actually of the same tile taken from different angles and some had been taken after he had moved the tiles to carry out the repairs in November.
In his application to the court, Greenhall said there appeared to be cracks in tiles in parts of the roof where the protesters had not gone. He added that Richardson’s method to date the cracks was not reliable and that he was only asked to look in one area when “what should have been done is an examination of the entire roof”.
“It’s clear this is a roof where there is pre-existing damage in areas where the protesters did not go. This is not a pristine roof by any means,” he said. “The simple fact that there are cracks in the tiles on the southern elevation by itself cannot be enough to get over the criminal standard that the defendants are responsible for it.”
He said that Richardson’s business relationship with the couple and responsibility for repairs at their house meant he “could not be described as being independent”.
During the trial, Scott Hall, the family’s personal chief of staff, said the property was “well-maintained” and staff “would have been aware of any damage to the roof”.
In cross-examination, Hall accepted there appeared to be some cracks in areas of the roof away from the protest that he had not been aware of and that some of the window frames appeared to have peeling paint.
Staff at the property were “shocked” to find Greenpeace activists in the grounds on the morning of August 3.
Speaking outside the court, Grant said: “Justice and common sense prevailed in court today, but that hasn’t been the case for many activists recently.
“We have become a country that regularly sends peaceful protesters to jail, with some facing years behind bars for trying to preserve a habitable planet for us all. This has to stop.
“Peaceful protest is a vital part of our democracy — it gave us votes for women, the right to a weekend and bans on commercial whaling and fracking.”
He said the activists had targeted Sunak’s home because it was a “personal” decision for him to issue new fossil fuel licences, and that they had made sure the family were not at home before the protest.

https://www.thetimes.com/travel/advice/t.title: Travel chaos 2024: all the strikes and disruption expected across Europe
https://www.thetimes.com/travel/advice/t.text:
This year has had its fair share of travel disruption with the usual strikes by airline, airport and rail staff the biggest causes alongside a barrage of other problems. Protests by organisations such as Just Stop Oil and unexpected airport evacuations have hampered some getaways and there’s the continuing possibility of airlines not having enough planes, giving rise to schedule changes and higher prices. Ryanair cancelled several flights scheduled for Tuesday, September 24, due to planned strikes at Italian airports, with destinations affected including Milan, Rome, and Venice.
If you are planning a much-needed break, here’s what you need to know about possible disruption.
Become a subscriber and, along with unlimited digital access to The Times and The Sunday Times, you can enjoy a collection of travel offers and competitions curated by our trusted travel partners, especially for Times+ members
Airline or airport strikes are almost inevitable during the busy summer season. Air traffic control strikes can be particularly problematic, as they’ll affect flights both in and out of a country, and any planes flying over its airspace.
There’s little you can do, except to ensure your airline has the correct contact details for you so that they can get in touch if there is a last-minute delay or cancellation. It’s also worth downloading your airline’s app, which will often contain information not available elsewhere.
On Tuesday, September 24, industrial action involving ground security personnel and baggage handlers affected airports in Bologna, Milan, Rome, and Venice. As a result of the 24-hour industrial action, Ryanair announced on September 23 that it had cancelled a “small number” of flights to and from these airports.
Passengers affected by cancellations or schedule changes were notified of their options via email and the Ryanair app, the airline said.
EasyJet said that it anticipated “delays and some disruption” due to the industrial action and advised passengers to continue to check the status of their flight online.
There are no strikes currently planned for the UK.
It’s worth bearing in mind that rail strikes could also affect your journey to or from UK airports, though there are currently none planned.
There are no strikes currently planned for France. The last strike involving French air traffic controllers, due to take place on April 24, was called off at the last minute after a pay deal was reached.
On Tuesday, September 24, industrial action involving ground security personnel and baggage handlers affected airports in Bologna, Milan, Rome, and Venice. As a result of the 24-hour industrial action, Ryanair announced on September 23 that it had cancelled a “small number” of flights to and from these airports on September 24.
There are currently no airport or airline strikes planned in Spain. In general, Spanish law requires minimum service levels to be met, which means the effect of strikes is usually limited.
There are currently no airport or airline strikes planned in Greece.
Issues at Boeing have impacted its production schedule over the summer, which means some airlines don’t have as many aircraft as they originally anticipated. Ryanair, for example, cut some of its summer schedule because of the delay. Wizz Air also had to cut its summer schedule because of required engine checks for its Airbus planes. The cumulative effect of this aircraft shortage means fewer flights, more expensive fares and potentially longer delays if an aircraft is taken out of service at the last minute.
• Boeing 737 Max: which airlines use them and how dangerous are they?
If air travel wasn’t already blighted with enough obstacles, there may also be further protests by Just Stop Oil on the horizon. The activist group has already targeted UK airports this year, including Stansted, where two private jets were sprayed with orange paint. In July, protesters blocked a security gate at Gatwick’s south terminal using suitcases with lock-on devices.
Air traffic control strikes and those by airport staff not directly employed by an airline are considered “extraordinary circumstances”, which means you won’t be due any compensation from the airline. However, airlines still have certain legal obligations and a duty of care if you’re already travelling.
If your flight is cancelled then the airline needs to either offer you a full refund for the journey, as well as for any affected return flights on the same booking, to be reimbursed within seven days, or offer you an alternative flight, including with a rival airline in some cases.
• Everything you need to know about compensation for cancelled and delayed flights
If your flight is delayed for an extended period, the airline needs to provide you with a reasonable amount of food and drink, a means for you to communicate, accommodation if your flight isn’t until the next day, and transfers to and from the accommodation.
In some cases, you’ll be provided vouchers for these items but often you are expected to claim back reasonable expenses from the airline afterwards, so keep your receipts.
You could still end up with out-of-pocket costs and, in this instance, a comprehensive travel insurance policy may be handy. Whether you’ll get a payout will depend on your coverage, so check the small print. Also, make sure you get something in writing from the airline to confirm the cause of the delay or cancellation.
• A guide to travel insurance: everything you need to know
On Friday, July 5, Heathrow Terminal 2 was evacuated by emergency services after the Metropolitan Police were alerted to a “suspicious item that needed to be checked out”. The incident was investigated and resolved, with no further action taken, but passengers affected by the evacuation were instructed to check with their airline regarding any disruption to their flights.
Airport evacuations such as this one are, on the whole, uncommon. However, in case of an emergency, airports do have plans in place for mass evacuations, and you should follow all instructions given by airport and airline staff. Following the evacuation, airports and airlines should keep you informed of developments via their official channels.
If your flight is delayed or cancelled as a result of the evacuation, you should check your airline’s policies to see if it offers compensation or refunds. Passengers should also consult their travel insurance policy details, as some providers might provide compensation for any disruption incurred as a result of the evacuation.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Rachel Reeves’s speech and the attack of the 50ft bifold grin
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Chancellor’s Labour conference attack on Tories was frankly immaculate even though she repeated key phrases 20 times
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
The chancellor’s big speech was introduced by a businesswoman called Alexandra Depledge, founder of a company that specialises in hassle-free home extensions. Within seconds you could see why.
There are two semi-detached houses around the corner from me where the owners clubbed together on a joint kitchen extension, both with giant quadruple bifold doors. I’ve been known to walk past it and say it’s the widest thing I’ve ever seen. But now I’ve seen Rachel Reeves’s brand new smile I won’t be saying that again.
The Labour Party is fighting very hard to shake off this freebie scandal, so it won’t help that it is impossible not to speculate whether Depledge was in some way involved in sourcing the architect and the building firm who must have assisted in grafting this never-seen-before 50ft grin on to the chancellor’s face.
• Labour conference as it happened
It’s permanent too. We know that because whatever she said, the smile remained. At the start, it kind of worked. Rachel Reeves is happy indeed to be the first Labour chancellor for 15 years and the first female one ever, so why not crack a smile? But when she moved on to the tub-thumping oratory about “building a Britain our daughters and our granddaughters can be proud of” the double kitchen-sized gnashers began to look more than a little unsettling.
Imagine Mel Gibson’s William Wallace riding up and down in front of his troops in Braveheart, roaring about no one taking away their freedom, but with his face fixed into a vacant smile that could otherwise have got him work as an extra in One Flew Over The Cuckoo’s Nest and you might get the general idea.
The only thing that broke Reeves’s smile, in the end, was a protester rising from the stalls to unfurl a flag of some sort. As with Sir Keir Starmer’s glitter-touting attacker this time last year, these protesters seem unable to explain to the many people in the room quite what is they’re protesting about. I know I could probably google it, but the wi-fi is terrible and the phone signal even worse and it just doesn’t seem worth the bother.
• Reeves: Trickle-down era is over, but winter fuel cuts here to stay
There is no clearer sign that the Labour Party is past being a party of protest than the sound of the room erupting with delight as the man with the banner was shoved with brute force towards the exit. We must therefore assume that Reeves and Starmer will act with a similar lack of squeamishness the next time Extinction Rebellion requires unglueing from the North Circular.
That was not the only moment of commotion either. To show they mean business, Labour has hosted a conference within a conference, specifically for business people, to which access is severely restricted. Before Reeves began speaking, the kind-of-a-big-deal business delegates were marched in to sit in a special roped-off area.
Well, I say roped off. The velvet rope was a length of white duct tape that became less sticky each time its minder raised and lowered it. I warned him: “Someone’s going to trip over that in a minute.” I was wrong. It took a lot less than a minute.
For reasons only Reeves can truly understand, her speech was structured around a two-sentence slogan: “That’s the Britain we’re building. That’s the Britain that I believe in.” She must have said it 20 times. It hardly needs to be stated that history’s most famous quotations tend only to have been said once. If JFK had said “Ich bin ein Berliner” a dozen times or more he might have looked like a bit of a wally, but he didn’t. If you are going to say something 20 times, why not make it something that isn’t vacuous?
• Good times ahead if we seize them, insists Reeves
Her biggest ovation by far was for her passionate promise to claw back billions in Covid fraud. They clapped so loud that no one could hear a word she was saying — which was just as well. They will probably still be clapping like mad when it becomes extremely clear it will be almost impossible to achieve.
The attacks on the four Tory leadership hopefuls were short, precise and frankly immaculate. She also spoke with real pride about giving public-sector workers, “the first proper pay rise they’ve had in 14 years”. It was a big decision. She’s right to own it, not avoid it. “If the Conservatives want to have a fight over who can be trusted with public services,” she said, “then I say: Bring. It. On.”
• Pace of growth falters amid worries about budget
It was by far the best bit. In a few weeks’ time someone from the Tory party is going to have to bring it on. It’s won’t be as easy as recent headlines might have them believe.
What will make it even harder for the Conservatives is the gift they keep on giving. For reasons only she can understand, Liz Truss decided to mark the occasion by reminding the nation that it was the second anniversary of the mini-budget, which definitely would have worked if it “hadn’t been undermined by the economic establishment”. Of late, Starmer has looked like a lucky general whose luck has run out. He need worry no more. There’ll always be Truss.
Back in Liverpool. By the time Reeves got to the very end, she’d had so many soaring conclusions it was hard to believe it was still going. Her final paragraph was a glorious Woolworths’ pick’n’mix of closing lines, including “Britain’s best days lie ahead”. Theresa May used to say that. It didn’t quite work out. “This time it’s going to be different though, because that’s the Britain I’m building. That’s the Britain I believe in.”
When Reeves said it for the 25th time it started to feel as if she was reading out the lyrics to When You Believe. Who can blame her? It’s a great song. Only time will tell whether it turns out to be the Mariah Carey and Whitney Houston version or the Leon Jackson cover.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.title: Coriolanus review — David Oyelowo can’t save this curiously flat production
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.subtitle: In Lyndsey Turner’s staging at the Olivier in the National Theatre you’ll spend more time looking at Es Devlin’s designs than admiring the grandeur of Oyelowo’s warrior
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre.text:
★★☆☆☆
For many people, Ralph Fiennes acquired the mantle of the ultimate warrior in the updated film version of Shakespeare’s martial tragedy. Tom Hiddleston won admirers, too, when he took on the role in Josie Rourke’s chamber version at the Donmar.
Can David Oyelowo, who brought the apostle of peace, Martin Luther King, to the big screen, match that steely level of testosterone? Sadly, no. Part of the problem with Lyndsey Turner’s curiously flat production is that you spend a lot more time casting an eye over the levitating grey slabs of Es Devlin’s characteristically chic set design than admiring the stiff-necked grandeur of Oyelowo’s doomed warrior. True, he dispatches one enemy with his shield, yet at crucial moments when he should be displaying his snarling contempt for his foes, this soft-spoken general has the quietly exasperated manner of a middle manager overwhelmed by a late-night pile of spreadsheets.
Turner presents us with a mostly modern-dress version of Rome where the governing elite confer in the bowels of what looks like a museum dressed up in Barbican Centre swathes of concrete. Busts of classical heroes, vases and a sculpture of Romulus and Remus being suckled by a wolf form the backdrop to the political intrigue. When we first see the handful of plebeian rioters, they are skulking around the display cases like members of Extinction Rebellion undertaking another of their special ops.
Rory Stewart provides one of the programme notes, written from his vantage point at this summer’s Democratic Convention in Chicago. But the production says little about the foibles of modern politicking. Ash J Woodward’s wall-size video designs do possess a certain grandeur: at the very end Coriolanus’s corpse is seen from above as it is carried away, arms outstretched like Christ on the cross. But the news bulletin-style video interludes that punctuate the action earlier look distinctly hackneyed.
Among the ensemble, shouting often takes the place of poetry. Nor is there much sense of intimacy between the hero and his domineering mother, Volumnia, played by Pamela Nomvete. Kobna Holdbrook-Smith’s rival commander Aufidius is a lacklustre presence as well: we never get much sense of the bond that draws the two men together. Peter Forbes’s Menenius does have a patrician sheen, though, and the ever-reliable Jordan Metcalfe brings a comic touch to Brutus, the conniving tribune who flits around like an over-zealous, tieless Spad.
That said, there was a surprising amount of laughter from the audience at other key scenes. At least Tim Lutkin’s intense lighting adds immediacy to the battle scenes, while Tom Gibbons’s rich sound design compensates for some of the humdrum verse speaking. Real flames flicker all around the stage at one point. What a pity there’s no fire at the heart of this offering.
165 minutes
